Matthew 21:19: "Let no fruit grow on thee henceforward for ever" (KJV).
Song of Songs 2:13: fig leaves and fruit as a sign of spring. Seasonal images are common in Scripture.

Futurists who link the fig tree to Israel answer that the leaves picture national revival, not yet spiritual fruit. They say fruit comes later when Israel turns to the Messiah (Zechariah 12:10). Other futurists reject the Israel link entirely and read Matthew 24:32 as a simple seasonal lesson.
Does "withered from the roots" (Mark 11:20) mean the roots stayed alive?
No. The fulfilled reading says "from the roots" includes the roots. The tree died completely, unlike Nebuchadnezzar's tree, whose stump was kept alive on purpose.

Some prophecy writers argued that only the trunk, branches and leaves died, while the roots stayed alive for a later revival. On the fulfilled reading, the phrase means the opposite. A tree withers "from the roots" because the roots have died. In normal Greek and English, "from" includes the starting point. The generations "from Abraham to David" include Abraham (Matthew 1:17). Herod killed boys "from two years old and under" (Matthew 2:16). Compare Daniel 4. There God ordered a tree cut down but told them to leave "the stump of its roots in the earth" with a band of iron (Daniel 4:15). That tree was kept for a later restoration (Daniel 4:26). Read this way, Mark gives no such hint for the fig tree.
Daniel 4:15, 26: the stump is left on purpose, and Nebuchadnezzar's kingdom is restored.
Job 18:16: "his roots shall be dried up beneath" (KJV). Withering roots mean full death.

Most futurist scholars do not use the "living roots" argument. They ground a future for Israel in Romans 11 instead, where Paul speaks of a root and branches that can be grafted back (Romans 11:16-24). They read the fig tree curse as a judgment on that generation, not on the people forever.
Does "no fruit from you ever again" really mean never, or only for an age?
In Greek the phrase stacks negatives with "to the age". Standard grammars call this a strong, emphatic "never". The fulfilled reading says it was a final curse.

Some writers say the Greek word aion means an age. So, they argue, Jesus only cursed the tree for a period. On the fulfilled reading, this ignores the rest of the sentence. Matthew 21:19 joins the strong negative "ou me" with "no longer" and "to the age". Mark 11:14 has "no longer", "to the age" and "no one". Grammars describe this piling up of negatives as a very strong denial. The same phrase "eis ton aiona" with a negative appears when Jesus says the believer will "never" die (John 11:26) or thirst (John 4:14). Read this way, Jesus' words to the tree were a full curse. If the fig tree is Israel's temple order, that order would never bear fruit again.
John 11:26: "shall never die" uses the same negative with "to the age".
John 10:28: the sheep "shall never perish". No one reads this as "only for a period".

Futurists answer that the curse applies to the tree and the temple order of that day, not to the Jewish people's future. They point to Romans 11:11, "did they stumble so as to fall? By no means". Many covenant theologians agree that the curse was on the old temple system, not on Jewish people as such.
If the fig tree is cursed, does that mean no Jewish person can bear fruit for God?
No. The fulfilled reading applies the curse to the old covenant order and its leaders. Individual Jews, like Gentiles, can bear good fruit through faith in Christ.

The fig tree pictures the nation's leaders, temple and system in that generation. It does not say anything against Jewish people as persons. Jeremiah saw both good figs and bad figs among the exiles (Jeremiah 24:1-10). John the Baptist told the crowds that every tree, Jew or not, would be judged by its fruit (Matthew 3:7-10). Jesus praised Nathanael as "an Israelite in whom is no guile" (John 1:47). The first church was almost wholly Jewish, and it bore great fruit (Acts 2:41; Acts 21:20). Paul, a Jew, said God had not rejected his people (Romans 11:1). On the fulfilled reading, the curse ended a covenant order, not God's love for a people. Every person, of any nation, is welcomed by faith in Christ (Romans 10:12).
Acts 21:20: "many thousands of Jews" believed in Jerusalem.
Romans 11:1: Paul calls himself an Israelite to prove God has not rejected his people.

All Christian views agree on this point. Dispensationalists go further and say God has a distinct national future for Israel. Many covenant theologians expect a large future turning of Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:25-26). Others read "all Israel" as the full number of Jewish and Gentile believers.
Should a metaphor be the key sign for all end-time prophecy?
The fulfilled reading says no. A central doctrine should rest on plain statements, not on a picture whose meaning Jesus himself explained as seasonal timing.

Popular futurism has made Israel's rebirth the starting point of end-time events. Yet the New Testament never says plainly that Israel would become a state again. So the fig tree verse is asked to carry the weight. On the fulfilled reading, this is a weak base. Jesus explained his own picture. Leaves mean summer is near; "so also" these signs mean the end is near (Matthew 24:32-33). He then gave the time frame: "this generation" (Matthew 24:34). Read this way, using the image to point to 1948 adds a meaning the text does not give. It also produced failed dates. Some writers used 1948 plus a forty-year generation to set the end near 1988. When 1988 passed, the scheme had to be revised.
1988: Edgar Whisenant's booklet predicted the rapture that year, partly by counting a generation from 1948.
Matthew 24:33: "so likewise ye". Jesus himself states what the picture means.

Many futurist scholars agree that the fig tree should not be used to set dates. They say Israel's return rests on Old Testament texts, such as Ezekiel 37 and Zechariah 12. Historic premillennialists and amillennialists also reject date setting, but differ on whether modern Israel has any prophetic meaning.
Does the Bible predict a future "bloodbath" for Israel?
The fulfilled reading says the predicted great suffering of Jerusalem already happened in AD 66-70. Jesus warned that generation to flee, and there is no further holocaust to wait for.

In a 1976 book Charles Ryrie wrote of a coming time of Israel's greatest bloodbath. He saw the Bible as history written in advance. The fulfilled reading agrees that Jesus predicted terrible suffering for Jerusalem (Matthew 24:21; Luke 21:23-24). But it holds that this judgment has already happened. Jesus told the people of Judea to flee to the mountains when they saw the signs (Matthew 24:16). Many Christians did leave before the siege. Josephus records famine, civil war and great loss of life (Jewish War 5.12.3; 6.9.3). His total of 1,100,000 dead is probably too high, but the scale was vast. Read this way, the Bible does not foretell another slaughter of Jews. Placing that suffering in the future can make it seem fated, which is dangerous.
Luke 21:20-21: "when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies ... flee".
Eusebius, Church History 3.5.3: Jerusalem's Christians moved to Pella before the war.

Dispensationalists hold that Zechariah 12-14 and Daniel 12:1 describe a future time of trouble for Israel. They stress that it ends in rescue and national conversion (Zechariah 12:10; Romans 11:26). They do not welcome suffering; they see Christ coming to save Israel. Many amillennialists apply these texts to the church's trials.
Is it antisemitic to deny that the Bible predicts a restored national Israel?
No. The fulfilled reading says antisemitism is hostility or prejudice toward Jews as Jews. A disagreement about how to read prophecy is not hatred of any people.

Some writers have said that anyone who denies a future national restoration of Israel is antisemitic. The fulfilled reading answers that this confuses theology with prejudice. Antisemitism means hostility, hatred or discrimination against Jewish people because they are Jewish. A person can read Old Testament restoration texts as fulfilled and still love and defend Jewish neighbours. On this reading, the restoration promises were kept in two stages. First came the return from Babylon (Ezra 1:1-4). Then came the gathering of Israel's faithful remnant into the Messiah's people, starting with thousands of Jews at Pentecost (Acts 2:41; Acts 15:15-17). Gentiles were grafted into that Jewish root (Romans 11:17-18). Read this way, the church is not anti-Jewish. Its foundation stones are Jewish apostles (Ephesians 2:20).
Acts 15:15-17: James applies the rebuilding of David's tent to Gentiles joining the Jewish church.
Romans 11:18: "you do not support the root, but the root supports you" (paraphrase).

Many Christian Zionists say that "replacement" readings have fed contempt for Jews in church history, and that a future for national Israel guards against this. Many Jewish scholars also see "supersession" as harmful. Most covenant theologians reject the label "replacement" and say the church is Israel enlarged, not Israel replaced.
Has dispensationalism itself changed on Israel and the church?
Yes. Since the late 1980s, "progressive dispensationalism" has softened the sharp split between Israel and the church. The fulfilled reading sees this as evidence that the older system was weak.

Classic dispensationalism, spread by the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) and Dallas Theological Seminary, taught two peoples of God with two programs. In the late 1980s and 1990s, scholars such as Craig Blaising, Darrell Bock and Robert Saucy developed "progressive dispensationalism". It sees more unity between Israel and the church. It accepts that Christ's Davidic reign has already begun in part (Acts 2:30-36). It is less focused on land and future dates. The fulfilled reading sees these changes as a move toward its own position. On this reading, the older system needed revision because its texts would not support the sharp divide. Peter, for example, says David's throne promise was fulfilled when Christ rose and sat at God's right hand (Acts 2:30-31).
Acts 2:30-36: Peter links David's throne to Christ's resurrection and ascension.
1993: Blaising and Bock published "Progressive Dispensationalism", and Saucy published "The Case for Progressive Dispensationalism".

Progressive dispensationalists say their changes refine the system, not abandon it. They still hold a future for national Israel in the land. Classic dispensationalists think the progressives gave up too much. Covenant theologians welcome the move toward unity but say it does not go far enough.
Where are the Old Testament promises to restore Israel fulfilled, on this reading?
In the return from exile, and then in Christ and the Jewish church he gathered. Gentile believers were later added into that same people.

The fulfilled reading sees two stages. First, God brought Judah back from Babylon as Jeremiah promised (Jeremiah 29:10). The temple and walls were rebuilt (Ezra 6:15; Nehemiah 6:15). Second, the deeper promises of a new heart and new covenant came true in Jesus (Jeremiah 31:31-34; Hebrews 8:8-13). The first church was almost all Jewish (Acts 2:5, 41). Gentiles were later grafted into this existing tree (Romans 11:17). The New Testament then calls all believers in Christ Abraham's seed (Galatians 3:7, 29), the true circumcision (Philippians 3:3), and members of "the commonwealth of Israel" (Ephesians 2:12, 19). Read this way, Israel was not discarded. Its faithful remnant became the core of a renewed Israel, open to all nations.
Hebrews 8:8-13 quotes Jeremiah's new covenant and applies it to the church.
Acts 2:5-11: Jews "from every nation under heaven" were gathered at Pentecost.

Dispensationalists say the new covenant was made "with the house of Israel" and still awaits a national fulfilment. The church shares only its spiritual blessings. Many covenant theologians agree with the fulfilled reading here but also expect a future mass conversion of Jewish people (Romans 11:25-26), as Charles Hodge and John Murray taught.
Does Zechariah 13:8-9 predict that two-thirds of Jews in Israel will die in the future?
Many futurists say yes. The fulfilled reading says the prophecy follows the striking of the Shepherd (13:7) and was fulfilled in the first century, so no future slaughter is foretold.

Zechariah 13:8-9 says two parts in the land will be cut off and die, and a third will be refined like silver. Some futurist writers apply this to a future tribulation. They have said two-thirds of the Jews in Israel will be killed. Israel has over seven million Jewish citizens today, so that would mean millions of deaths. On the fulfilled reading, the context places the text in the past. Zechariah 13:7 says "strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will scatter". Jesus applied this to his own arrest (Matthew 26:31). The refining that follows fits the generation after the cross, ending in AD 70. A refined remnant called on God's name and became his people (Zechariah 13:9; Romans 11:5). Read this way, no future holocaust is required by Scripture.
Matthew 26:31: Jesus quotes Zechariah 13:7 on the night he was arrested.
Josephus, Jewish War 6.9.3: huge loss of life and 97,000 taken captive during the war.

Dispensationalists hold that Zechariah 12-14 forms one future scene. In it the nations attack Jerusalem, Israel mourns for the pierced one (12:10), and Christ returns (14:4). They stress that the surviving third is saved, and that God, not believers, brings the trial. Some amillennialists read the two-thirds and one-third as a picture of judgment and remnant in every age.
Does the "parenthesis" view mean God has no dealings with Israel today?

The fulfilled reading argues that the classic view, by pausing God's program for Israel until the rapture, logically leaves present Israel without special prophetic status. Dispensationalists strongly reject that conclusion.

Classic dispensationalism teaches that God's prophetic clock stopped after 483 years of Daniel's seventy weeks (Daniel 9:24-27). The church age is a "parenthesis". The final seven years, "the time of Jacob's trouble" (Jeremiah 30:7), will begin after the rapture. One Scofield companion said God is not dealing with Israel as a nation during this age. The fulfilled reading draws out an implication. If Israel's promises are postponed, then Jewish people today stand before God like everyone else. Their hope is in Christ (Romans 10:12-13). Read this way, the fulfilled reading is not saying anything harsher than the parenthesis view. Both agree that salvation for Jew and Gentile is in Christ alone. The difference is about the future of a nation.
Romans 10:12: "there is no difference between Jew and Greek".
Daniel 9:24-27: the seventy weeks, read with a gap by dispensationalists and without one by the fulfilled reading.

Dispensationalists answer that Israel remains "beloved for the fathers' sake" and that God's gifts and calling cannot be revoked (Romans 11:28-29). They say the Abrahamic promise to bless those who bless Israel (Genesis 12:3) is still in force. They see the regathering of Jews to the land as God preparing for the coming week.
Did end-times expectation make some Christians passive during the Nazi persecution of Jews?
A historian from within premillennialism found that many premillennial writers in the 1930s saw the persecution as expected and said little against it. Others, from many traditions, did help Jews.

In 1977 Dwight Wilson, a lifelong premillennialist, studied American premillennial writing on Russia and Israel since 1917. He found that many premillennial writers saw European antisemitism in the 1930s as a forerunner of "Jacob's trouble". Some treated it as part of God's plan. Wilson judged that this led to a fatalistic "hands off" attitude, with little moral protest. Some writers even blamed Jews for their own suffering. Wilson also said premillennialists were, in theology, more pro-Jewish than any other Christian group. On the fulfilled reading, this history shows the danger of treating persecution as a fixed future event. Read this way, the Bible calls Christians to resist injustice, not to watch it (Proverbs 24:11-12). Fairness requires adding that wider society also failed refugees then.
1939: the ship St. Louis, carrying over 900 Jewish refugees, was turned away by Cuba, the United States and Canada.
Proverbs 24:11-12: "rescue those being led away to death" (paraphrase).

Defenders note that apathy toward refugees was widespread among Christians and governments of every view. They point to premillennialists who aided Jews, and to the strong support for Israel among dispensationalists since 1948. Historians such as Timothy Weber and David Rausch differ on how much fundamentalists shared the antisemitism of their time.
Did some prophecy teachers accept the forged "Protocols of the Elders of Zion"?
Yes. Historians record that a few leading dispensational teachers in the 1920s-30s gave credit to the Protocols, a forgery exposed in 1921. Others in the same movement rejected it.

The Protocols claimed to reveal a Jewish plan for world control. In 1921 The Times of London showed that much of it was copied from an 1864 French satire about Napoleon III. Henry Ford spread it in his newspaper, the Dearborn Independent, in the early 1920s. In 1927 Ford publicly apologised. Historian Timothy Weber records that James M. Gray, president of Moody Bible Institute, defended parts of Ford's claims in 1927. He was criticised by Jewish groups and by Hebrew Christians. Arno C. Gaebelein, a Scofield Bible editor, treated the Protocols as genuine in his 1933 book. He also led a mission to Jews in New York. On the fulfilled reading, this shows how prophecy speculation can mix with prejudice. The Bible forbids false witness against any neighbour (Exodus 20:16).
August 1921: The Times (London) exposed the Protocols as plagiarised from Maurice Joly's 1864 satire.
1927: Henry Ford issued a public apology and closed the series.

Defenders of dispensationalism point out that the system's founders were strongly pro-Jewish, and many teachers condemned the Protocols. Historian David Rausch argued that most early fundamentalists were friends of the Jewish people. All Christian traditions today reject the Protocols, and all have their own history of antisemitism to repent of.
Why could a teacher love Jewish evangelism yet repeat harmful ideas about Jews?

The fulfilled reading says the system expected both future Jewish suffering and future Jewish salvation, so both attitudes could live side by side. Historians also point to the wider prejudice of that era.

Some early twentieth-century teachers ran missions to Jewish people while repeating damaging claims about Jews in world events. Historians have asked why. One answer is that their prophecy system expected Jews to pass through a terrible tribulation before turning to Christ. This could make persecution seem both expected and part of God's plan. The fulfilled reading argues that this is a built-in risk of placing "Jacob's trouble" in the future. Read this way, a past fulfilment removes that risk. The great tribulation is over, so no modern suffering is "prophesied". Jews today should be treated like any neighbour: with love, honesty and respect (Romans 13:10). Paul's own longing for his people is the model (Romans 9:1-3; Romans 10:1).
Romans 9:2-3: Paul's "great sorrow" for his Jewish kin.
Romans 10:1: "my heart's desire and prayer ... for Israel is that they might be saved" (KJV).

Many historians say these men reflected the prejudices of their whole culture, not of one view of prophecy. Antisemitism also appeared among Christians of other eschatologies, and in liberal and secular circles. Dispensationalists today stress that God's love for Israel, not its suffering, is the heart of their view.
If futurists expect great suffering in Israel, why do some encourage Jews to move there?
The fulfilled reading asks this as a pointed question. It contrasts it with Jesus' warning to leave Jerusalem before its fall (Matthew 24:16).

Some Christian groups have helped Jews immigrate to Israel and have funded settlements. They believe the Bible foretells a regathering in the last days. Yet many of the same teachers expect that two-thirds of Jews in the land will die in a future tribulation (Zechariah 13:8). One commentator also read Zechariah 14:2 as a future defeat of Jerusalem by all nations. The fulfilled reading asks why Jews are not being warned to flee. Jesus told his hearers to flee Judea when the signs came (Matthew 24:16; Luke 21:21). On this reading, the New Testament never urges anyone to gather in Jerusalem for the end. It points to a new worship not tied to that city (John 4:21-24). Read this way, a future-focused system creates a painful tension.
Luke 21:21: "let those in the city depart" (paraphrase).
John 4:21: "neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem" will you worship the Father.

Christian Zionists answer that they help Jews because God promised to bless those who bless Abraham's seed (Genesis 12:3). They see the return as God's own act (Ezekiel 36:24). They believe the coming trial ends in the Messiah's rescue (Zechariah 14:3-4). They say they do not cause the tribulation and pray for Israel's peace (Psalms 122:6).
Did the guilt of "all the righteous blood" (Matthew 23:35-36) rest on Jews of every age?
No. Jesus limited it to "this generation". On the fulfilled reading that judgment fell in AD 70 and ended. No later Jew carries it.

Jesus told the leaders of his day that the blood of the righteous, from Abel to Zechariah, would come "upon this generation" (Matthew 23:35-36). The fulfilled reading stresses the limit. It was that generation, which rejected its visitation (Luke 19:44). The judgment fell in AD 66-70 and was complete. Sadly, church history shows Christians blaming Jews of later centuries as if the guilt never ended. The fulfilled reading says this is a misuse of Scripture. Ezekiel taught that a son does not bear his father's guilt (Ezekiel 18:20). Read this way, placing Jesus' judgment in its own generation actually protects Jewish people from a false charge. It leaves no room for treating Jews today as cursed.
Ezekiel 18:20: "the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father" (KJV).
1965: the Catholic document Nostra Aetate stated that Christ's death cannot be charged against all Jews then living, or against Jews today.

Most Christians of every view now agree that Jews of later ages carry no guilt for the crucifixion. Futurists also limit the judgment of Matthew 23 to that generation. But some apply the larger "times of the Gentiles" (Luke 21:24) to the long dispersion that followed, and expect a future end to it.
How has "His blood be on us and on our children" (Matthew 27:25) been misused?
It was used for centuries to call Jews "Christ-killers". On the fulfilled reading, the cry touched only that crowd and their children in AD 70, and Peter offered that same generation forgiveness.

In Matthew 27:25 a crowd in Jerusalem cried that Jesus' blood would be on them and their children. Through the centuries some Christians used this verse to blame all Jews for Jesus' death. This fed hatred and violence. The Passion play at Oberammergau, Germany, first performed in 1634, was criticised for this theme. It was revised in later decades. On the fulfilled reading, "our children" were the next generation, who lived through AD 70 (Luke 23:28). The words do not reach further. Even so, Peter told Jerusalem's people that the promise of forgiveness was "for you and your children" (Acts 2:38-39). Jesus prayed, "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34). Read this way, the gospel answers that cry with mercy, not a lasting curse.
Luke 23:28: "weep for yourselves and for your children". Jesus' warning about that generation.
Acts 2:39: "the promise is unto you, and to your children" (KJV).

Christians of all views now reject the deicide charge. Many teachers stress that all humanity, Jew and Gentile, put Christ to death (Acts 4:27). They note that Roman authority carried out the execution. Some scholars also point out that the crowd was small compared to the whole nation.
Is it right to call the Holocaust God's punishment on the Jewish people?
No. On the fulfilled reading, the covenant judgment Jesus foretold ended in AD 70. Scripture gives no warrant for calling later atrocities divine punishment.

In 1990 a leading Israeli rabbi suggested the Holocaust was a punishment for sin. Many in Israel were outraged, including survivors. One survivor said the remark turned the killers into God's messengers. Some Christian writers have also said that Israel remains under divine discipline until it turns to Christ. On the fulfilled reading, such claims misuse prophecy. Jesus' warning of judgment had a time limit, "this generation" (Matthew 24:34), and it was fulfilled. Jesus also warned against reading disaster as proof of special guilt (Luke 13:1-5; John 9:2-3). Read this way, the murder of six million Jews was a monstrous evil by human beings. It was not the fulfilment of a prophecy. Its authors bear full guilt before God (Genesis 9:6).
Luke 13:4-5: those killed when the tower fell were not worse sinners than others.
1941-1945: about six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust.

Christians of all views condemn the Holocaust as great evil. Some futurists hold that Israel as a nation is under discipline until it believes (Romans 11:25), but most firmly deny that this excuses or explains the Holocaust. Jewish thinkers have debated the question deeply, and most reject the idea of punishment.
Is sharing the gospel with Jewish people antisemitic?
The fulfilled reading says no. The apostles, who were Jews, preached to Jews first. Respectful witness is love, though coercion and contempt are wrong.

In 1989 an evangelical gathering issued the Willowbank Declaration, urging Christians to share the gospel with Jewish people. A rabbi with the American Jewish Committee called it a blueprint for spiritual genocide. Jewish concern is understandable. In history, Jews were sometimes forced to convert, as in Spain in 1391 and 1492. The fulfilled reading draws a line. Forced conversion and contempt are sins. But a free, kind invitation is not hatred. Peter, Paul and the other apostles were Jews who preached first to Jews (Acts 3:25-26; Romans 1:16). Paul longed for his people's salvation (Romans 10:1). Read this way, both the fulfilled reading and dispensationalism agree that Jews, like all people, are welcome in Christ.
Acts 3:25-26: Peter says God sent his servant "to you first".
1492: the Alhambra Decree forced Spain's Jews to convert or leave.

Some Christians hold a "two-covenant" view, that Jews are saved through God's covenant with Israel apart from Christ. They avoid evangelism for that reason. Most evangelicals, dispensational or not, reject this view (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). Many Jewish leaders see targeted missions as a threat to Jewish survival after the Holocaust.
Is criticism of the State of Israel's policies the same as antisemitism?
Not in itself. Disagreeing with a government is different from hostility to a people. But criticism can become antisemitic when it uses double standards or old hatreds.

The fulfilled reading says opposing policies of Israel's government is not the same as opposing Jews. In the Cold War, many Christians opposed the Soviet state while respecting the Russian people. Christians can ask whether any state acts justly, including its treatment of Christians and Arabs. But care is needed. Criticism becomes antisemitic when it blames all Jews for a government's acts. It does so when it uses old stereotypes, or holds Israel to standards applied to no other nation. On this reading, the Bible calls for just weights for everyone (Proverbs 11:1; Leviticus 19:15). Read this way, a Christian may be neither a blind supporter nor an enemy. He can pray for peace for all who live in the land (Psalms 122:6-8).
Leviticus 19:15: judge the poor and the great alike, without partiality.
Micah 6:8: do justice, love mercy and walk humbly with God.

Christian Zionists often say God's promises give the State of Israel special status, so opposing its existence opposes God's plan (Genesis 12:3). Many Jewish groups warn that anti-Israel rhetoric often hides antisemitism. Other Christians, including many Palestinian Christians, say biblical justice requires honest critique of all governments.
What is the real Christian answer to antisemitism?
Love of neighbour. The fulfilled reading says the issue is ethics, not end-times charts: every Jewish person bears God's image and must be treated with justice and love.

Minority groups of many kinds have been mistreated in history. In the United States, enslaved Africans suffered terribly, and Irish immigrants faced job barriers. Jewish people have faced hatred in nearly every century. On the fulfilled reading, no view of prophecy can protect them by itself. The answer is obedience to God's moral law. Every person is made in God's image (Genesis 1:27). We must love our neighbour as ourselves (Leviticus 19:18). Jesus taught that a neighbour can be of any race or faith (Luke 10:29-37). Paul warned Gentile believers not to boast against Jewish branches (Romans 11:18-20). Read this way, Christians of every eschatology must stand against hatred of Jews. Here all the views agree.
Luke 10:33: the hero of the parable is a Samaritan, from a despised group.
Romans 11:18-20: Gentile believers must not be proud, but fear.

Christian Zionists add that standing with Israel as a nation is part of this love (Genesis 12:3). Many Jewish and Christian scholars say churches must also face the history of anti-Jewish teaching in sermons and texts. Most traditions now teach respect for Judaism and reject the contempt of the past.
Should the views of the early church fathers settle questions of prophecy?
No. On the principle of Scripture alone, the fathers are helpful witnesses but not final judges. If the Bible says something happened in the first century, it happened.
